records.title: Development of an exploratory preoperative laboratory-based score for 24-month mortality after major lower extremity amputation in geriatric diabetic foot patients
records.abstract: Major lower extremity amputation for diabetic foot complications is associated with substantial mortality, particularly in older adults. We evaluated whether routinely available preoperative laboratory parameters provide prognostic information for 24-month mortality and developed an exploratory laboratory-based risk score.  This retrospective cohort study included 72 patients aged ≥ 65 years who underwent transtibial or transfemoral amputation for diabetic foot complications between January 2021 and June 2023 at a tertiary referral center. Vital status was ascertained through July 31, 2025. Associations with 24-month all-cause mortality were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression. A 3-point score was derived from laboratory predictors using receiver operating characteristic analysis and Youden-index-based thresholds. Model discrimination and calibration were assessed, and bootstrap optimism correction was applied to the fixed three-biomarker Cox model. The proposed score was additionally compared with the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI), Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI), and Hemoglobin–Albumin–Lymphocyte–Platelet (HALP) score.  Thirty-nine patients (54.2%) died within 24 months. Kaplan–Meier-estimated 24-month survival was 45.8% (95% CI 34.1–56.8%). In multivariable Cox analysis, higher hemoglobin (adjusted HR 1.302, 95% CI 1.041–1.628; p = 0.021), lower platelet count (adjusted HR 0.9966, 95% CI 0.9939–0.9994; p = 0.017), and lower albumin (adjusted HR 0.868, 95% CI 0.813–0.927; p 10.3 g/dL, platelet count p  A simple score based on albumin, hemoglobin, and platelet count showed promising prognostic discrimination for 24-month mortality after major amputation in this geriatric diabetic foot cohort. Quantitative ischemia severity and standardized neuropathy and frailty assessments were unavailable, and the score was derived and evaluated in the same derivation cohort, while bootstrap optimism correction was limited to the fixed three-biomarker Cox model. It should therefore be regarded as exploratory, should not replace comprehensive clinical and vascular assessment, and requires external validation before clinical use.

records.title: Impact of malnutrition and protein-enriched oral nutrition on early recovery after fragility fractures in older adults: the NuTra trial
records.abstract: Malnutrition is highly prevalent in geriatric trauma patients and is associated with impaired recovery, complications, and reduced likelihood of returning home. Nonetheless, the impact of a targeted protein-enriched diet during the acute hospital stay on patient outcome and rehabilitation remains to be investigated. Materials and  This single-center randomized controlled study enrolled patients ≥ 70 years with fragility fractures admitted to a Level I trauma center. Nutritional status was assessed using the Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 and Mini Nutritional Assessment. Patients screened positive in ≥ 1 tool were classified as being at nutritional risk and randomized to a protein-enriched diet (Group A) or standard diet (Group B); patients with negative screening served as observational reference group without nutritional risk (Group C). The intervention targeted 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day protein. Primary outcomes were in-hospital medical complications, surgical site infections and functional mobility at discharge. Secondary outcomes included length of stay, discharge destination, and in-hospital mortality. Multinomial logistic regression assessed independent associations with discharge destination.  Of the 218 patients (mean age 81.8 ± 6.9 years; 72.0% female), 100 (45.9%) screened positive for being at nutritional risk and were randomized to intervention (A, n = 46) or control (B, n = 54), while 118 (54.1%) patients without nutritional risk served as reference group (C). Patients at nutritional risk showed higher comorbidity burdens, higher ASA classes, and greater frailty than group C. Medical complications occurred in 45.0% of patients, with no significant differences between groups. Serum albumin decreased and CRP increased during hospitalization, without differences among the groups. Patients in reference group C were more often independently mobile and discharged home, whereas all patients at nutritional risk more frequently required institutional care. In multivariable analysis, a higher age-adjusted CCI was independently associated with discharge destination, whereas no independent effect of the nutritional intervention was observed.  In this geriatric trauma cohort, being at nutritional risk was closely linked to frailty and multimorbidity. A protein-enriched diet during the acute hospital stay did not translate into measurable short-term benefits regarding complications, functional mobility, length of stay or discharge destination. Nutritional risk should therefore be considered within the broader context of overall vulnerability, and nutritional care may need to be embedded in comprehensive longitudinal rehabilitation strategies extending beyond the acute in-hospital phase. Trial registration The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov on 12 May 2026 (NCT07582575).

records.title: Activity diversity and psychological richness across midlife and older adulthood
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Psychological richness, a dimension of well-being characterized by novelty, complexity, and perspective change, is theoretically grounded in varied and unusual experiences. Daily reports were drawn from two cohorts of the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study: MIDUS 2 (M2; N = 1,834) and the MIDUS Refresher (MR; N = 730). Daily activity diversity was quantified with Shannon entropy, capturing both the breadth and evenness of participants' daily activities. records.title: Crossing the Digital Divide: Understanding Older Adults’ Technology Acceptance of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Qualitative Study
records.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
records.abstract: The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence is redefining the relationship between older adults and digital technologies. Existing studies have largely explained the digital divide among older adults through traditional digital media such as smartphones and mobile payment, while insufficient attention has been paid to how conversational artificial intelligence changes older adults’ entry thresholds, sustained-use motivations, and risk-judgment mechanisms. This study adopts a multimethod qualitative design, with semistructured interviews as the primary method and digital scenario-based tasks as a complementary method. From January to February 2026, the study was conducted in Chedun Town and Xinqiao Town, Songjiang District, Shanghai, with 40 participants aged 60 and above who had internet-use experience and showed a pronounced tendency toward high-frequency smartphone use. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis. Interview transcripts, task-observation records, screenshots of AI conversations, and field notes were triangulated; an initial coding manual, double review, and consensus discussion were used to enhance analytic credibility. The study finds that generative artificial intelligence shifts the technological threshold from procedural operation to need articulation and result evaluation, enabling some older adults to compensate for limitations in traditional interface operation through life experience and language-expression skills. Older adults’ sustained use is not driven simply by efficiency, but is closely related to emotional anchoring in later life, experience organization, relationship maintenance, and concrete task handling. Community support, peer learning, and intergenerational assistance constitute important mediating mechanisms through which older adults move from initial experimentation to stable use. Whether older adults truly cross the digital divide depends on whether they can develop the capacities of source verification, contextual delimitation, and boundary judgment. Based on these findings, the study proposes a “conditional crossing” mechanism for older adults’ acceptance of AI technologies and argues that age-friendly governance should move beyond interface simplification toward capability enhancement and risk support.

records.title: Age-associated differences in lower-extremity muscle mass, force, and power in older adults: a cross-sectional analysis of sex differences
records.abstract: The decline in musculoskeletal function with aging is a key contributor to mobility impairments and loss of independence. While sarcopenia and dynapenia are well described, recent evidence highlights muscle power as a more sensitive indicator of functional deterioration. Aims This study aimed to compare age-associated differences in muscle mass, force, and lower-limb muscle power in older adults over different assessment , while accounting for sex-related differences.  Three hundred nineteen community-dwelling adults aged 60–97 years were assessed for muscle mass (DXA-derived lean mass, appendicular skeletal muscle mass index), muscle force (handgrip force, knee extension maximal isometric contraction), muscle moments and angular velocity (isokinetic dynamometry), and lower-limb muscle power (isokinetic testing and sit-to-stand power). Associations with age and sex were examined using regression models and ANOVA.  Lower-limb muscle power showed a stronger negative association with age than muscle force or mass (β = − 0.433 vs. − 0.303 and − 0.119, respectively; p  Lower-limb muscle power appeared more sensitive to age-associated differences than muscle force or mass, supporting its role as a key biomarker of neuromuscular aging. This study also highlights that sex may contribute to variability in age-associated patterns of muscle power, raising questions about the universality of its definition that warrant further confirmation. These findings emphasize the clinical importance of including power assessments in strategies to preserve independence in older adults. records.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and agreement of calculated serum osmolarity for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients, using clinical impression of dehydration as the reference standard, and to examine glucose levels across concordant and discordant classification groups. Design and setting This prospective, observational study was conducted in a geriatric acute care unit. Participants The study included 455 older hospitalized patients with a mean age of 82.2 ± 6.8 years and 70% were female. Measurements Clinical impression of dehydration (dehydration vs. no dehydration [normal hydration + hyperhydration]) was judged and recorded by the attending physician within 24 h of admission. High calculated osmolarity occurred in 38%. Using the ≥ 295 mOsmol/l cut-off, sensitivity was 48.6% and specificity 65.1%; positive and negative predictive values were 29.7% and 80.7%, respectively, and accuracy was 61.3%. Agreement beyond chance was poor (κ = 0.112). Mean glucose was higher in osmolarity-positive groups, including false positives (all p  In older hospitalized patients, calculated serum osmolarity (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) showed limited agreement with clinical dehydration assessment with frequent osmolarity-positive classifications in clinically non-dehydrated patients. These findings support cautious clinical interpretation of calculated osmolarity in acute care, particularly when glucose is elevated.

records.title: Body weight following a multidomain lifestyle intervention in older adults at risk of dementia – A post-hoc analysis of the AgeWell.de-trial
records.abstract: Lifestyle interventions provide a promising approach to address higher body weight as a risk factor for dementia.  The AgeWell.de-trial was primarily designed to preserve cognitive function and reduce dementia risk. In this post-hoc analysis, we investigated body weight following the multidomain intervention among older adults with overweight or obesity, as well as the role of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss.  Analyses used data from the cluster-randomized AgeWell.de-trial, testing a multidomain intervention (dietary counselling, enhancement of physical, social and cognitive activity, medication review, intervention for cardiovascular risk factors, depressive symptoms/grief, if applicable) over 24 months in adults aged 60 to 77 years at risk for dementia. Associations between intervention allocation and body weight at follow-up were analyzed using linear regression, controlling for covariates, based on multiply imputed data.  The sample included n = 678 participants with a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m², mean age (SD): 68.9 (4.8), 52.1% female. Group allocation was not associated with body weight at 24-month follow-up (b (unstandardized regression coefficient) = -0.30, 95% CI: -0.51; 1.11). Older age (b = -0.14, 95% CI: -0.25; -0.03) and a high level of education (b = -1.28, 95% CI: -2.55; 0.00) were linked to lower body weight at follow-up, while higher baseline body weight predicted higher body weight at follow-up (b = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.91; 0.98). Levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss remained high but stable in both groups, regardless of group allocation.  In this post-hoc analysis, group allocation was not associated with lower body weight at follow-up. Despite high levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss and favorable changes in diet and physical activity in the intervention group, these changes did not translate into measurable weight loss. Trial registration AgeWell.de was prospectively registered in the German Clinical Trials Register on December 7th, 2017 (DRKS trial identifier DRKS00013555).

records.title: Two-assessment patterns of past-year hospitalization reporting and subsequent functional deterioration and mortality among older adults in China: a two-window longitudinal prognostic factor study
records.abstract: Past-year hospitalization reports may identify older adults with adverse subsequent prognosis, but two assessments do not continuously observe hospital use and their incremental information beyond one-wave reporting is uncertain.  We analysed two three-wave windows of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS): 2011 (Wave 1) and 2013 (Wave 2) hospitalization reports with 2015 (Wave 3) outcomes, and 2013 (Wave 2) and 2015 (Wave 3) reports with 2018 (Wave 4) outcomes. Patterns were 00 (neither assessment), 01 (second only), 10 (first only) and 11 (both). The prespecified primary analysis compared 11 with 00 for survivor-conditional ADL deterioration (increase ≥1) among participants with observed outcome-assessment ADL. Modified Poisson models used community-clustered robust covariance and 50 multiply imputed datasets. Four-pattern, one-wave, mortality, composite, sequential complete-covariate, cognition missing-not-at-random (MNAR), and inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting (IPCW) analyses were also examined.  ADL deterioration occurred in 932/4,365 observed survivors in Window 1 and 961/4,911 in Window 2. Adjusted RRs for 11 versus 00 were 1.230 (95% CI 1.007–1.502) and 1.094 (0.906–1.320), respectively. RRs for 11 versus pooled 01 + 10 were 1.229 (1.000–1.511) and 1.019 (0.845–1.228). Mortality RRs were 1.461 (0.986–2.166) and 1.482 (1.187–1.849), and death-or-deterioration RRs were 1.240 (1.054–1.459) and 1.166 (1.031–1.319). In fixed complete-covariate sequential analyses, 11-versus-00 point estimates moved markedly toward or below the null after multidimensional health adjustment, with wide confidence intervals. Cognition MNAR estimates changed little; IPCW point estimates were similar in magnitude (Window 1 RR 1.222, 95% CI 0.999–1.494; Window 2 RR 1.092, 0.905–1.317).  The 11 pattern marked less favorable prognosis relative to 00, but the survivor-conditional functional association varied across calendar windows and analytic strategies, and two reports did not consistently distinguish risk from one-wave reporting. These related within-cohort windows do not constitute independent replication.  support cautious prognostic interpretation, not a causal effect, verified recurrent-admission measure or stand-alone screening rule.

records.title: Enhanced person profiles: a cluster randomised trial protocol for Swiss long-term care facilities
records.abstract: Family participation and teamwork are crucial components of person-centred dementia care in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) and are therefore widely recommended. However, these often remain ad hoc and staff-dependent in LTCF settings. Robust evidence on reproducible whole-team models for family participation and their impact on the quality of life of people with dementia is limited. The person profile is a complex intervention that has been tested under randomised controlled trial conditions, but family participation and teamwork were identified as weak areas in this intervention. Consequently, we developed the enhanced person profile. This programme incorporates clinical tools for routine family participation and psychological safety  that enhance teamwork, ultimately aiming to improve the quality of life of people with dementia.  We will conduct a two-period, two-sequence cluster randomised crossover trial in 20 LTCFs in German-speaking Switzerland with 260 people with dementia. Each period will last 7 months, separated by a 1-month washout. Clusters will follow one of two sequences (intervention → usual care or usual care → intervention). The primary outcome will be proxy-rated quality of life (QUALIDEM). Secondary outcomes will comprise symptoms and concerns (Integrated Palliative Care Outcome Scale for People with Dementia (IPOS-Dem)), person-centred care (Person-Centred Practice Inventory – Staff Short Form (PCPI-S SF)), perceived family participation (FICS-T), and teamwork (Team Climate Inventory (TCI); unit). Our analyses will be carried out using linear mixed-effects models under the intention-to-treat principle, accounting for clustering and repeated measures. A mixed- process evaluation will be employed to examine implementation, mechanisms, and context, with qualitative follow-up exploring sustainability. Discussion This trial, embedded in routine LTCF care, will assess the effects of the enhanced person profile on the quality of life of people with dementia and determine its mechanisms of action as well as implementation requirements for large-scale adoption. Trial registration This trial was registered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00041653). The Berne Cantonal Ethics Committee (lead committee) reviewed and approved the protocol and study documents, including the consent forms, educational materials, and electronic case report forms (BASEC-ID: 2026 − 00761).

records.title: Physical, psychological, and cognitive multimorbidity patterns and the risk of disability among older adults in China: a prospective cohort study
records.abstract: Physical disorders frequently co-occur with psychological and cognitive conditions, increasing the risk of disability. However, the specific disability risks associated with distinct multimorbidity patterns remain unclear. This study aimed to examine the differential risks of disability associated with various combinations of physical, psychological, and cognitive disorders.  Data were obtained from the 2018 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, involving 5186 adults aged 60 and older with a 2-year follow-up. Modified Poisson regression models were utilized to assess associations between multimorbidity patterns and disability risk, stratified by age and sex. Relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated.  Five disease patterns were identified: only physical disorders, psychological or cognitive disorders, physical-cognitive multimorbidity, physical-psychological multimorbidity, and physical-psychological-cognitive multimorbidity. Compared to participants without disorders, four patterns were significantly associated with disability after two years. Specifically, physical-psychological-cognitive multimorbidity presented the highest risk (aRR = 4.02, 95%CI:2.94–5.50), followed by physical-psychological multimorbidity (aRR = 3.30, 95%CI:2.40–4.54), physical-cognitive multimorbidity (aRR = 2.20, 95%CI:1.60–3.03), and only physical disorders (aRR = 1.85, 95%CI:1.36–2.52). Subgroup analyses by age and sex yielded consistent .  This study demonstrates a graded increase in disability risk among older adults in China across various combinations of physical, psychological, and cognitive disorders, particularly when psychological conditions coexist with physical illnesses. These findings suggest that emotional and cognitive screenings should be integrated into routine geriatric assessments.

records.title: Local RAGE Inhibition Attenuates Early Diabetic Retinal Pathology in Streptozotocin-Induced Rats
records.abstract: Introduction Diabetic retinopathy, which occurs during extended periods of chronic hyperglycemia, is one of the main causes of vision loss. The receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) plays a central role in inflammatory and angiogenic signaling, both of which contribute to the pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy, but its therapeutic targeting in ocular disease has been insufficiently explored.  We evaluated topical RAGE229, a small-molecule RAGE inhibitor, and an intravitreally administered anti-RAGE antibody in a streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat model. At day 84, treatment effects were assessed using masked fundoscopic scoring, RT-qPCR, immunohistochemistry, and histological morphometry. Treated eyes were evaluated against both route-matched diabetic vehicle-control groups and paired contralateral vehicle-treated eyes.  Both interventions reduced fundoscopic pathology and retinal Vegfa and Nfkb1 expression, whereas Ager showed only a non-significant downward trend. NF-κB p65 immunoreactivity was reduced by both treatments, while a significant reduction in VEGF-A immunoreactivity was detected only in the paired anti-RAGE antibody analysis. Morphometric analysis indicated attenuation of diabetes-associated retinal thinning with both interventions. Neither intervention altered systemic glycemic control. Although both interventions demonstrated similar overall anatomical protection, anti-RAGE antibody treatment showed more consistent effects across protein-level and structural endpoints.  These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence that local RAGE-targeted treatment may attenuate vascular, molecular, and structural manifestations of early experimental diabetic retinopathy without detectable changes in systemic glycemia. Further preclinical studies should evaluate ocular exposure, direct target engagement, functional visual outcomes, and reproducibility in larger cohorts.

records.title: Gaps Between Self-Reported and Documented Use of a Health Care Service Portal Among Older Adults: Cross-Sectional Survey and Retrospective Electronic Data Study
records.abstract: Health care systems increasingly offer services to citizens through online portals, which have been found to be associated with patient satisfaction and better management of health concerns. Few studies have compared self-reported use with objectively documented portal use, especially among older adults.  This study aimed to examine differences between documented and self-reported health portal use, and their associations with  variables and digital health literacy (DHL) among older adults.  A cross-sectional telephone survey was conducted among 600 participants aged 60 years and older, who were sampled from a registry of members of a national health maintenance organization (HMO). The participants reported their use of the HMO’s portal, their DHL, and demographic and  variables. Participants’ use of the portal was retrospectively retrieved from the HMO’s administrative database.  A large gap between self-reported use and documented use of the health portal was found: for example, while only 8.1% (46/566) reported not using the portal, the HMO’s records indicated that 62% (372/600) did not make use of the portal. However, a positive correlation was found between self-reported use and documented use ( r =0.22; P r =0.41; P r =0.56; P P =.02) and ethnicity (β=−0.22; P r =0.09; P= .04), was not significantly associated with documented use in this analysis (β=0.02; P =.97).  The findings indicate that users tend to overestimate their health portal use. Interpretations vary from measurement issues, such as social desirability bias regarding digital functioning or the perception that assisted use also constitutes usage, to signaling their identity as engaged digital health consumers. Future studies on digital health use should also include measures of electronically documented use and not only self-reported use.

records.title: Real-world evidence on the management and outcomes of glioblastoma in elderly patients: a monocentric retrospective analysis
records.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) carries a poor prognosis, and older patients and those with impaired performance status are often underrepresented in randomized trials. This study evaluated real-world treatment patterns, survival outcomes, and factors associated with outcome in older patients with GBM.  We retrospectively analyzed 63 patients aged ≥ 65 years with a diagnosis of GBM managed at a single-center radiation oncology department between 2014 and 2023. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were calculated from diagnosis. Multivariable Cox models included age, sex, Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), radiologically confirmed gross total resection (GTR), and temozolomide (TMZ) administration as clinically prespecified covariates. Complete-case analyses were performed. Proportional hazards assumptions were assessed using Schoenfeld residuals, with additional time-varying and exploratory sensitivity analyses addressing diagnostic classification, treatment selection, concomitant TMZ exposure, and treatment timing.  Median OS was 7.0 months (95% CI 5.3–14.4) and median PFS was 5.3 months (95% CI 3.9–7.8). In the multivariable OS model ( n = 56; 50 deaths), increasing age was associated with higher mortality (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.02–1.17; p = 0.011), whereas female sex was associated with a lower hazard of death (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.23–0.91; p = 0.025). Omission of TMZ was associated with higher mortality (HR 2.26, 95% CI 1.16–4.41; p = 0.017), while GTR showed a directionally favorable association that did not reach conventional statistical significance (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.27–1.01; p = 0.054). In the PFS model ( n = 56; 53 events), increasing age (HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01–1.14; p = 0.027) and omission of TMZ (HR 2.34, 95% CI 1.20–4.55; p = 0.013) were associated with higher hazards, whereas female sex (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.23–0.89; p = 0.022) and higher KPS (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.96–1.00; p = 0.039) were associated with lower hazards. Resection status violated the proportional hazards assumption for PFS; time-varying analysis indicated an early favorable association of GTR that attenuated over time. Sensitivity analyses based on concomitant TMZ exposure and survival measured from radiotherapy initiation yielded similar associations.  Survival remained limited in this real-world cohort of older patients with GBM. Age, sex, performance status, resection status, and TMZ administration showed varying associations with outcome, with TMZ showing the most consistent association across analyses. Given the small retrospective cohort and substantial treatment selection, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than causal.

records.title: Frailty and outcome after hospital admissions in two populations aged 80 years and above in 2012 and 2022 using the Hospital Frailty Risk Score
records.abstract: Purpose To study outcomes in two cohorts of patients ≥ 80 years admitted to a tertiary hospital in Bergen Norway in 2012 and 2022.  This retrospective observational study compared two separate calendar-year cohorts of patients aged ≥ 80 years hospitalized in 2012 and 2022. Frailty was assessed using the ICD-10-based Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS). Outcomes included hospital length of stay, 30-day readmission, hospital mortality, and one-year survival after last admission. Survival was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier curves and Cox regression models.  There was an increase in patient admissions from 5112 (2012] to 6232 (2022] with a female majority. Half of both cohorts were classified as frail [HFRS > 15], with no significant sex difference. Non- frail patients had the highest one-year survival [87%] compared to 69% in the high frailty group. A higher mortality was found in frail males [65%] compared with females and in the age group ≥ 90 years. The combination of high frailty risk [HFRS > 15], age ≥ 90 years and male had the lowest survival of all sub-group analyzed [60%].  Higher HFRS was associated with worse clinical outcomes. The HFRS was able to identify vulnerable patient groups with significantly increased mortality, but there was no increase in frailty over the 10-year period in the two cohorts.

records.title: Efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens in pulmonary tuberculosis patients aged 70 years and above: a retrospective study
records.abstract: Older patients aged 70 years and above exhibit immunosenescence, increased comorbidity burden, and high susceptibility to adverse drug reactions. The standard HRZE regimen remains controversial in this population due to the considerable toxicity of pyrazinamide (PZA). This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone (FQ)-containing triple or quadruple regimens compared with conventional standard HR(L2)ZE or HR(L2)E regimens in older pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) patients, so as to provide evidence for individualized treatment strategies in older adults.  A total of 184 newly diagnosed PTB patients aged ≥ 70 years were enrolled in this single-center retrospective study in 2023. Patients were divided into four groups according to initial anti-tuberculosis regimens: standard HR(L2)ZE quadruple therapy group, HR(L2)E triple therapy group, FQ-containing quadruple group, and FQ-containing triple group. Treatment outcomes and adverse event rates were compared among groups. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to identify independent risk factors for treatment failure and adverse events. Propensity score matching (PSM) was further performed between the standard HR(L2)ZE and FQ-containing quadruple groups to minimize baseline selection bias.  Significant differences in treatment success rates and overall adverse event rates were observed among the four groups ( P P  For PTB patients aged 70 years and older, the conventional HR(L2)ZE standard regimen is associated with high toxicity and limited clinical applicability. FQ-containing triple and quadruple regimens were associated with more favorable treatment outcomes, while PZA omission was associated with a lower risk of adverse events. Individualized therapeutic strategies with prudent PZA use and rational selection of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens may be considered for older patients. Given the retrospective observational design and potential selection bias, the observed associations should not be interpreted as causal relationships and require confirmation in prospective multicenter studies. records.title: Effects of multicomponent exercise combined with nutritional intervention on global cognitive function and depressive symptoms in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.abstract: To systematically evaluate the effects of multicomponent exercise (ME) combined with nutritional intervention on global cognitive function and depressive symptoms in older adults.  A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published from inception to June 30, 2026. Participants were older adults aged ≥ 60 years. Interventions were required to include both ME and nutritional intervention. Primary outcomes were global cognitive function and depressive symptoms. Hedges‘ g was used as the effect size measure, and a random-effects model was prespecified as the primary model for all pooled analyses. Subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses were also performed.  A total of 9 RCTs involving 1,814 participants were included. Of these, 7 studies contributed data on global cognitive function and 5 studies contributed data on depressive symptoms. Meta-analysis showed that ME combined with nutritional intervention may improve global cognitive function ( g = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.08 ~ 0.54) and depressive symptoms ( g = -0.51, 95% CI: -0.93~-0.09) in older adults, but moderate-to-high heterogeneity was observed in both global cognitive function ( I² = 68.54%) and depressive symptoms ( I² = 63.54%) analyses. Subgroup analyses showed no statistically significant between-subgroup differences by nutrition type, baseline cognitive status, or exercise modality ( P > 0.05), and only intervention duration showed a significant subgroup difference for global cognitive function ( P  ME combined with nutritional intervention may have a small beneficial effect on global cognitive function and depressive symptoms in older adults. However, the current evidence is limited by the small number of included studies, moderate-to-high heterogeneity, underpowered subgroup analyses, and potential publication bias. The trim-and-fill-adjusted estimates for both global cognitive function and depressive symptoms were attenuated, and their 95% confidence intervals crossed zero, indicating sensitivity to potential publication bias. These  should be regarded as exploratory and interpreted with caution. Future high-quality RCTs with larger sample sizes, longer follow-up periods, and standardized intervention protocols are needed for validation.

records.title: Toward Standardization of Intrinsic Capacity Assessment: A Methodological Comparison of the Responsiveness of Composite Scoring Methods
records.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used as an intervention outcome; however, IC composites lack a standardized scoring method, hindering comparisons across trials. To determine whether the scoring method influenced the detection of intervention effects, we applied multiple composite scoring approaches to the same data and compared their responsiveness to a 12-week exercise intervention in older adults at risk of mild cognitive impairment. : Pre- and post-intervention IC data were obtained from 59 community-dwelling older adults assigned to resistance training (n=34) or stretching and flexibility (n=25). The five-domain IC composite was computed repeatedly using alternative scoring approaches: z-score (concurrent and baseline-anchored variants), percentage of maximum possible (POMP), binary classification (0/1), and a three-category ordinal scale. Responsiveness was quantified using the standardized response mean (SRM). : Responsiveness ranged from negligible to large for identical data, indicating that the intervention effect depended on the scoring method. The ordinal and POMP composites were the most responsive (SRM 0.74–0.88 and 0.50–0.76). Within the z-score composite, responsiveness depended entirely on the standardization anchor: the concurrent specification was insensitive (SRM ≈ 0), whereas baseline-anchoring showed moderate responsiveness (0.62–0.71). The binary scoring was the least sensitive, showing a ceiling effect. : Ordinal three-category scoring was the most responsive, suggesting that approaches combining a fixed reference with a category-based structure are well suited for detecting change in IC. This finding requires confirmation against external criteria for IC, such as its predictive validity for adverse health outcomes, along with domain weighting and instrument selection.

records.title: Location, Location, Location: How Community Distress Shapes Physical and Mental Health Outcomes for Caregiving Grandparents
records.abstract: The health of caregiving grandparents is a critical area of research. Financial strain is a well-established predictor of health and a common issue for caregiving grandparents.  We sought to understand how community context influences this relationship between financial strain and health. Specifically, we examined two dimensions of community context: community distress and perceived access to key resources for caregiving.  Using a sample of caregiving grandparents ( N = 439), we first conducted Latent Class Analysis to identify distinct profiles of resource access. We then used moderated mediation analyses to test whether financial well-being mediated the relationship between community distress and health, and whether this indirect effect varied by resource access profile.  We found the relation between community distress and health through financial well-being varies depending on the grandparents’ perceived resource access. This research points to the importance of community context in the lives of grandparent caregivers.

records.title: Intrinsic capacity among Hispanic older adults in the United States: Sociodemographic correlates and subgroup analyses
records.abstract: and  Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used to conceptualize healthy aging. However, evidence on socio-demographic correlates in IC among Hispanic older adults in the United States remains limited. Research Design and  We analyzed data from a nationally sampled cohort from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study, including Hispanic adults aged ≥60 years. IC was constructed from five domains. Multiple linear regression models examined associations between socio-demographic factors and IC, with stratified analyses by gender, community of residence, and place of birth.  The sample included 749 participants (60.08% female; 89.05% urban residents; 63.02% foreign-born), with a mean IC score of 6.49 (SD = 1.67). records.abstract: Rural-to-urban migration separates many rural older adults from adult children and changes how care is received and experienced. Rural left-behind older adults remain in their rural places of origin after family members migrate for work.  This study examined conditional associations among reported care items and compared care networks by number of children and gender.  Cross-sectional data were obtained from 836 rural left-behind older adults aged 55 to 95 who completed the 14-item CSS-RLE. EBIC-LASSO Gaussian graphical models estimated item-level networks, expected influence summarized net signed connectivity, and network comparison tests assessed subgroup differences.  Village care and visits had the highest expected influence in the overall, male, and three-or-more-child networks. Holiday gifts from offspring ranked highest in the one- and two-child networks, whereas living expenses from children ranked highest in the female network. Network structure differed between one-child and larger-family groups and between men and women.

records.title: Ageism and Quality of Life in Older Adults: The Roles of Self-Disgust and Psychological Distress
records.abstract: This study examined psychological correlates of quality of life (QoL) among older adults in a Latin American context, focussing on the roles of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to examine the incremental contribution of sociodemographic factors, three dimensions of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress to QoL among 272 Colombian older adults (mean age = 68.40, SD = 6.80). Findings indicated that interpersonal experiences of ageism, but not exposure to ageist messages or self-ageism, were associated with poorer QoL. Higher self-disgust and psychological distress were independently associated with lower QoL and formed part of a significant indirect association between interpersonal ageism and QoL. These findings suggest that quality of life in later adulthood is associated not only with structural and sociodemographic conditions, but also with psychological processes through which age-related stigma may be experienced and internalised. Interventions that reduce interpersonal ageism while promoting self-acceptance and more positive views of ageing may represent promising avenues for supporting wellbeing and quality of life in older adults.

records.title: Intrinsic Capacity in a Nationally Representative US Population
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is defined by the World Health Organization as the sum of an individual’s physical and mental abilities that support health and well-being. While well validated internationally, it has not been operationalized and validated in a nationally representative US cohort.  Using data from 5,834 community-dwelling older adults from Round 12 (2022) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) survey, we identified measures related to IC domains (cognition, locomotion, vitality, psychological, sensory). We performed exploratory factor analysis (EFA), omega hierarchical reliability testing, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using bi-factor and second-order structures. We also constructed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) screening tool. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used to examine the associations of IC and ICOPE scores with demographic and health characteristics. Age- and sex-specific reference centile curves were developed using empirical percentiles.  EFA consistently supported a six-factor structure (vision and hearing were separate). Omega hierarchical analysis supported a strong general factor (ω = 0.92; ωₕ=0.72), and the bi-factor model demonstrated excellent fit. IC and ICOPE scores showed strong correlation (r = 0.71). Higher IC scores were associated with younger age, higher level of education, and income. Prevalence of comorbidities, frailty, ADL and IADL disability increased from the highest to the lowest IC and ICOPE quartiles. Reference centile curves demonstrated progressive age-related decline, with females showing lower IC scores than males.  We demonstrate IC operationalization in a nationally representative U.S. cohort and provide the first US-specific reference centile curves. The findings provide a foundation for future IC research in the US.

records.title: Exploring Heterogeneity in Smartphone Addiction Risk Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Guangzhou: A Machine Learning Analysis
records.abstract: Smartphone addiction risk is an underexamined concern in later life, and prior research often treats older adults as a homogeneous group. Using cross-sectional survey data from 2,275 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Guangzhou, this exploratory study applied XGBoost with SHAP analysis to identify predictive correlates, followed by K-means clustering to examine subgroup heterogeneity among participants classified as high risk. Social participation and depressive symptoms were associated with the risk with nonlinear patterns. Two exploratory profiles were identified: the Socially Active profile (40.7%), characterized by high participation and more regular non-kin contacts, and the Emotionally Withdrawn profile (59.3%), characterized by elevated depressive symptoms, fewer regular non-kin contacts, and entertainment-oriented use. The findings lend credence to the paradigms of social overload and emotional compensation and suggest that digital inclusion among older adults must be coupled with support for digital self-regulation, psychological well-being, and social and family engagements.

records.title: Deprescribing Fall Risk–Increasing Drugs in Older Adults: Implementation Challenges and a Conceptual Framework from the DeFRID Trial and Global Evidence
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Deprescribing fall risk–increasing drugs (FRIDs) is essential for reducing polypharmacy and falls in older adults, yet randomized controlled trials (RCTs) face unique implementation challenges. The DeFRID study is an ongoing multi-center RCT evaluating an ARMOR-based deprescribing intervention versus usual care in adults aged ≥60 years prescribed FRIDs. The  of this review are threefold: (1) to describe practical challenges encountered during a multi-center deprescribing RCT in India; (2) to propose a conceptual framework for categorizing these barriers; and (3) to contextualize DeFRID's experience within the broader deprescribing research landscape.  We conducted a narrative review with systematic scoping elements, synthesizing global RCT evidence from PubMed, OpenAlex, and Google Scholar (inception–December 2025) with DeFRID process evaluation data. DeFRID barriers and facilitators were identified via mixed- (clinician KAP questionnaire and qualitative interviews), team meetings, retention logs, and Phase II RCT implementation data, thematically categorized, then compared with global RCT challenges.  DeFRID implementation revealed four challenge categories: ethical–clinical difficulties establishing equipoise for FRID withdrawal; operational barriers to recruitment and retention; methodological complexities in fall outcome ascertainment; and context-specific constraints unique to the Indian LMIC setting—limited deprescribing guidelines, polypharmacy normalization, fragmented care coordination, and hierarchical decision-making. Global RCTs revealed substantial implementation challenges: low clinician adherence, short follow-up periods, restrictive eligibility excluding frail or cognitively impaired older adults, and resource-intensive interventions limiting scalability.  Deprescribing FRIDs in older adults is impeded by ethical, operational, methodological, and provider-patient challenges, necessitating multilevel strategies integrating training, shared decision-making, context-specific guidelines, and stakeholder engagement for scalable implementation.

records.title: Vulnerability Intersections: An Integrative Conceptual Framework for Understanding Vulnerability in AI-Assisted Care for Older Adults
records.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly used to support independent living and care for older adults, particularly those in vulnerable situations. Yet, how vulnerability is constructed when AI enters later-life care remains poorly theorized. Existing approaches to vulnerability in old age inadequately address AI-related risks, structural conditions, exposure pathways, and life course disadvantages. Using a theory-synthesis approach, this article proposes “vulnerability intersections” as an integrative framework for how vulnerability is constructed, enacted, and negotiated in AI-assisted care for older adults. The framework extends existing sociotechnical accounts by conceptualizing vulnerability as taking four overlapping forms: anticipatory, opaque, routinized, and normative. It locates vulnerability factors at the micro level of older adults’ lives, the meso level of care organizations and technology providers, and the macro level of political-economic and regulatory arrangements, with life-course accumulation spanning all three. It also proposes three exposure pathways through which vulnerability factors become consequential: AI-mediated information and representations of aging; AI-powered care organization and delivery; and AI-configured power, participation, and social relations. The framework shifts attention away from viewing older adults as inherently vulnerable toward examining the sociotechnical arrangements under which vulnerability is anticipated, classified, distributed, and negotiated when AI enters care.

records.title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients’ experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The  of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.  We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.  Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans’ sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians. Discussion Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.

records.title: Multimorbidity, Polypharmacy, and Neighborhood Disadvantage as Determinants of Cognitive Performance in the ARCHES Cohort
records.abstract: African American adults experience a disproportionate burden of dementia, shaped by structural and clinical factors that remain unclear.  To quantify associations between multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and cognition in the context of neighborhood disadvantage.  This study is a cross-sectional analysis of 348 African American adults aged 45–92 years (mean 64.3 years; 73.6% female) from the Aging Research Characterizing Health Exposome via Social drivers (ARCHES) cohort. Comorbidity burden was assessed using a modified Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), polypharmacy as ≥5 medications, and neighborhood disadvantage using the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). Linear regression estimated associations with a Preclinical Alzheimer’s Cognitive Composite (PACC). The polypharmacy model included modified CCI as a covariate, and effect modification by ADI was assessed using an interaction term between polypharmacy and ADI.  Higher modified CCI was associated with lower cognitive performance (B = −0.071; 95% CI: −0.130, −0.012). Polypharmacy was not independently associated with cognition after modified CCI adjustment (B = −0.081; β = −0.057; p = 0.257). No significant ADI interaction was found (p = 0.064).

records.title: Chronic inflammation and multiple dimensions of aging among women in the Philippines
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Age-related increases in chronic systemic inflammation are strong predictors of morbidity and mortality in high income countries, but evidence is lacking from lower- and middle-income settings where infectious diseases are more prevalent and rates of overweight and obesity are relatively low. Here we evaluate two complementary measures of chronic inflammation—plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) and a DNA methylation–based surrogate (DNAm-CRP)—measured at baseline as predictors of physical capacity, cognitive function, and cardiometabolic disease seven years later among women in the Philippines (N = 953; 43-75 years at follow-up). Levels of CRP and DNAm-CRP were not strongly associated with age. Both measures predicted subsequent declines in physical and functional capacity, increased incidence of diabetes and hypertension, and poorer cognitive performance, after adjustment for baseline status and other covariates. DNAm-CRP performed comparably to CRP, and was robust to variation in white blood cell composition and acute infectious symptoms at the time of sampling. These findings demonstrate that chronic inflammation is associated with multiple dimensions of aging in a lower-middle income setting, and highlights the utility of inflammatory biomarkers as scalable tools for global aging research.

records.title: Association of vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep in cognitively unimpaired middle-aged and older adults
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Low vitamin D and B12 levels are linked to low self-reported sleep quality and conditions comorbid with sleep disturbances in older adults. We examined the associations between serum vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep indices in middle-aged and older adults.  We studied 460 participants aged 40 and older (70.9 ± 12.0 [SD] years; 52.8% female; 22.2% Black) in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. Predictors included total serum vitamin D and B12, sleep outcomes included total sleep time (TST, minutes), sleep efficiency (SE, %), sleep onset latency (minutes), wake after sleep onset (WASO, minutes), and average wake bout length (WBL, minutes). We examined race and sex as effect modifiers of associations between vitamins and sleep.  Higher vitamin D concentration was associated with longer TST (B = 23.63 minutes, 95% CI, 9.62-37.64) and shorter WBL (B = −0.29 minutes, 95% CI, −0.50 to −0.09). Vitamin D deficiency was associated with shorter TST (B= −23.03 minutes, 95% CI, −42.05 to −4.01). The associations between vitamin D and sleep were stronger among Black participants. Higher B12 was associated with shorter WASO in women but longer WASO in men. B12 insufficiency/deficiency was associated with longer TST in men but shorter TST in women.  Higher vitamin D levels are associated with longer and less disturbed sleep in middle-aged and older adults. Future studies are needed to understand if maintaining optimal vitamin D levels improve sleep quality and promote better sleep-associated health outcomes.

records.title: Planetary Health Diet Adherence and Frailty in Older Adults: Evidence from the Seniors-ENRICA Cohorts
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Frailty is a major determinant of disability and adverse outcomes in older adults. The Planetary Health Diet (PHD), a plant-based dietary pattern promoting environmental sustainability, has been associated with lower mortality and reduced chronic disease risk. We examined the association between adherence to the Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) and frailty over time using repeated frailty assessments.  Data came from two cohorts of community-dwelling older adults: Seniors-ENRICA-1 (2008-2015; ≥60 years; n = 3,289) and Seniors-ENRICA-2 (2015-2023; ≥65 years; n = 3,273). Baseline diet was assessed using a validated diet history, and adherence to the PHD was assessed using the PHDI (0-140), based on 15 food groups. Frailty was defined by the Fried phenotype (≥3 criteria of exhaustion, low physical activity, slow gait, muscle weakness, unintentional weight loss). Generalized estimating equation (GEE) models estimated odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for frailty across PHDI tertiles, adjusting for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical factors.  Higher PHDI adherence was consistently associated with lower odds of frailty over time. Comparing highest vs. lowest tertiles, multivariable-adjusted ORs (95% CI) were 0.62 (0.42, 0.92) in Seniors-ENRICA-1, 0.40 (0.24, 0.65) in Seniors-ENRICA-2 and 0.52 (0.38, 0.70) in the pooled analyses. Higher PHDI adherence was primarily associated with lower odds of low physical activity, while vegetables and fruits showed the strongest independent associations among individual PHDI components.  Greater PHDI adherence is associated with lower odds of frailty in Spanish older adults, supporting the potential role of sustainable, plant-based dietary patterns for healthy ageing.
